intro: Chiara Bertoglio plays Schubert’s Impromptu in G♭ major, D. 899 No. 3, marked Andante, in which a long melody sounds above flowing broken chords and a bass line. The middle section moves into E♭ minor before the opening tune returns.

sections.label: A · Melody above triplets, G♭ major
sections.mNote: Long B♭ notes above G♭-major broken chords.

sections.label: B · Accented melody over E♭-minor bass
sections.mNote: The bass takes up the triplet motion.

sections.label: A′ · The G♭ melody returns
sections.mNote: The returning melody later adds new chromatic notes.

sections.label: Coda · G♭ over a descending bass
sections.mNote: The bass moves through E double-flat, D♭ and C♭.

relations.label: The G♭ melody returns
relations.basis: The outer melody returns after the contrasting E♭-minor-centred middle. The 218.5 s measured offset agrees with the A′ marker near 218 s; the later continuation and coda are not assumed identical. CENS diagonal mean 0.964, sustained 39.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 218.5 s (cache/form/schubert-impromptu-gflat.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening melody over broken chords
cues.text: The melody holds B♭ while broken chords turn beneath it. Lower still, the bass moves more slowly. One pianist plays melody, accompaniment and bass line together.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), bars 1–4; Ph. Raynaud’s Mutopia transcription, melody, inner broken chords and bass. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: E♭ minor passage, bars 25–28
cues.text: The music moves to E♭ minor. The B♭s in the melody now carry accents, and the bass adds rising triplets: E♭–F–G♭, then G♭–A♭–B♭.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), bars 25–28; Mutopia transcription: accented B♭ melody, E♭-minor broken chords and rising bass triplets. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First publication in G major, 1857
cues.text: When this Impromptu was first published in 1857, twenty-nine years after Schubert’s death, the publisher transposed it from G♭ major to G major. It is played here in the original six-flat key.
cues.evidence: IMSLP, 4 Impromptus D 899: Nos. 1–2 first published in 1827, Nos. 3–4 in 1857; Schubert’s holograph carries a pencil instruction, attributed by IMSLP to Carl Haslinger, to transpose No. 3 from G♭ to G. Original-key edition: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), transcribed by Mutopia, https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193. https://imslp.org/wiki/4_Impromptus,_D.899_(Schubert,_Franz)

cues.title: G♮ in the accompaniment
cues.text: G♮ replaces G♭ beneath the melody’s B♭, turning E♭ minor towards E♭ major. The broken chords continue.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), bars 48–51; the bass and broken chords introduce G♮. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: After the fermata, C♭ in the melody falls to B♭ and the bass rises from F to G♭. The opening melody returns, pianissimo, over the broken chords of the opening.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), bars 54–55: fermata, C♭–B♭ melody and F–G♭ bass. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Impromptus and Winterreise, 1827
cues.text: Schubert composed both sets of Impromptus in 1827, the year of Winterreise. He set the first twelve of Müller’s poems in February and the second twelve in October.
cues.evidence: IMSLP gives 1827 as the year of composition for both sets of Impromptus, D 899 and D 935, and “1827 February – Autumn” for Winterreise. Christian Utz, ZGMTH 18 (2021), note 13: Schubert set Müller’s poems in two phases eight months apart, February and October 1827, knowing only twelve poems in the first. https://imslp.org/wiki/4_Impromptus,_D.899_(Schubert,_Franz) https://imslp.org/wiki/4_Impromptus,_D.935_(Schubert,_Franz) https://imslp.org/wiki/Winterreise,_D.911_(Schubert,_Franz) https://www.gmth.de/zeitschrift/artikel/1132.aspx

cues.title: Chromatic inflection in the returning melody
cues.text: In bars 70–72 the returning melody rises from C♭ through D♭ to D♮, then falls from E♭ to E double-flat. The triplets continue underneath.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), bars 70–72; melody and continuing broken chords in the Mutopia transcription. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Falling bass in the coda
cues.text: In bars 75–77 the melody stays close to G♭ while the bass descends through E double-flat and D♭ to C♭. Beneath the sustained note the harmony is C♭ minor (C♭–E double-flat–G♭).
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), bars 75–77: bass descent and C♭–E double-flat–G♭ harmony. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Final cadence, bars 85–86
cues.text: The melody thickens into chords. Below it the broken-chord triplets make their last descent and stop. The final G♭-major chord is held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), bars 85–86; final triplets, G♭-major chord and fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: D♮ leads to E♭ minor
transitions.from: A · Melody above triplets, G♭ major
transitions.to: B · Accented melody over E♭-minor bass
transitions.how: Near the end of bar 24, D♭ becomes D♮ inside the broken chords, and the bass moves from G♭ to F. Bar 25 arrives on E♭ minor. B♭ in the melody carries an accent, and the bass begins to climb in triplets beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), bars 24–25, transcribed by Ph. Raynaud for Mutopia. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193

transitions.title: Fermata on the dominant seventh before the return
transitions.from: B · Accented melody over E♭-minor bass
transitions.how: A D♭ dominant seventh is held over F in the bass under a fermata. At the return, the melody’s C♭ falls to B♭ and the bass rises from F to G♭. The opening tune and its broken chords resume pianissimo.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), bars 54–55, transcribed by Ph. Raynaud for Mutopia. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193

transitions.title: Descending bass into the coda
transitions.to: Coda · G♭ over a descending bass
transitions.how: In bars 74–76 the bass descends from G♭ through F♭, E double-flat and D♭ towards C♭, while the melody above stays close to G♭. As the coda begins, the broken chords introduce C♭ minor, with E double-flat beneath.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel (1888), bars 74–76, transcribed by Ph. Raynaud for Mutopia. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1193

composer.epithet: Composer who at seventeen wrote a song for Gretchen with a spinning-wheel accompaniment and at thirty-one wrote music for two cellos.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition lessons with Antonio Salieri
School assistant; tutor to the Esterházy daughters at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; independent composer
The singer Vogl, the poets Schober and Mayrhofer, the painter Schwind, Josef von Spaun
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and stage works

quote.text: I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.
quote.source: Schubert to his friends about Winterreise, 1827, as Josef von Spaun later recalled; our translation

composer.background:
In the Schubert family quartet, Franz played the viola, his brothers the violins and his father the cello. He was born on 31 January 1797 in Himmelpfortgrund, a Viennese suburb, and grew up in his father’s schoolhouse. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer taught him further. At eleven he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school, where he played Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven in the school orchestra.

Salieri began teaching him composition in 1812. The next year Schubert left the boarding school, trained as a teacher and returned to his father’s classroom as an assistant. On 19 October 1814, aged seventeen, he wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade. In the piano part the right hand imitates the spinning wheel and the left hand the treadle, while Goethe’s Gretchen sings of her thoughts of Faust. At the point where she recalls his kiss, the accompaniment figure stops. The following year brought roughly 140 songs, among them Erlkönig, as well as church music, a symphony and works for the stage.
